passage:
The school van was honking downstairs and rain was hammering the window. "Madhuri, raincoat on. Now," said her mother, Gurpreet, holding it open.
"No!" Madhuri crossed her arms and sat down on the floor. "I don't want it."
Gurpreet took a breath. Then she held up two things instead. "Yellow raincoat or the umbrella with ducks? You pick."
Madhuri jumped up. "Raincoat! I do the buttons myself." She did them all wrong, laughed, and ran for the door.

qa.q: What two things did Gurpreet hold up?
qa.a: Gurpreet held up the yellow raincoat and the umbrella with ducks.

qa.q: Why do you think Madhuri said "No!" and sat on the floor?
qa.a: Being told "Now" felt like an order, so refusing let her feel in charge, even though she didn't really mind the raincoat.

qa.q: What worked for Gurpreet even with the van honking?
qa.a: Instead of repeating the order, she offered two options that were both fine, so Madhuri could choose and cooperate quickly.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurpreet when the van is honking and Madhuri refuses?
qa.a: Stressful 😅; she is in a hurry with rain pouring down, and she has to take a breath to stay calm instead of snapping.

grounding: It shows a preschooler refusing an order outright and then happily cooperating once she is offered a choice between two acceptable options.

passage:
In their flat in Pune, Yogesh knelt by the shoe rack. "Swati, sit. I'll put your sandals on, we're late for the vegetable market."
"I do it!" Swati pulled her foot away and hid both sandals behind her back. When he reached for them, she ran off to the balcony.
Yogesh sat back on his heels. Then he picked up the sandals and her pink shoes. "Which ones today, sandals or pink shoes? And do you want to put them on yourself?"
Swati came back at once, chose the pink shoes, and pushed her feet in, tongue poking out as she tugged at the straps.

qa.q: Where did Swati run when Yogesh reached for the sandals?
qa.a: Swati ran off to the balcony.

qa.q: What does Swati's "I do it!" suggest she wants?
qa.a: It suggests she wants to be in charge of her own feet; being told to sit while someone else did it made her push back.

qa.q: What could Yogesh keep doing on busy mornings?
qa.a: Offer two choices he is happy with and let Swati do the part she can manage, which turns a chase into quick cooperation.

qa.q: How might the morning feel different for Yogesh after he offers the choice?
qa.a: He goes from chasing Swati to the balcony to watching her happily tug her straps, so they can leave without a struggle.

grounding: It shows a preschooler refusing help because it was ordered, then complying happily when given a choice between two acceptable options.

passage:
"Raghav, eat your dal now. Open your mouth."
"No!" Raghav clamped his lips shut and turned his face to the wall.
"Just one spoon, beta."
"No, Hemant Dadu! No, no, no."
Dadu put the spoon down. "Hmm. Do you want the red spoon or the steel one?"
Raghav peeked over his shoulder. "Red."
"And do you want to hold it, or shall I?"
"Me!" He grabbed the red spoon and dug into the dal. "Look, Dadu, big spoon!"
"Very big," said Dadu, hiding a smile behind his hand.

qa.q: Which spoon did Raghav choose?
qa.a: Raghav chose the red spoon.

qa.q: Why did Raghav turn his face to the wall at first?
qa.a: Raghav felt cross and bossed about, being told to eat now and open his mouth, so saying no felt like his only way to have a say.

qa.q: Which choice helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking red or steel spoon and who should hold it; both options meant eating, but Raghav got to decide, so he ate happily.

qa.q: Why might Dadu hide a smile?
qa.a: He can see the same boy who refused a moment ago now proudly eating, and it amuses him how much a small choice changed things.

grounding: It shows a preschooler refusing to eat when ordered, then eating happily once he chooses between two acceptable options.

passage:
Teacher's note, Nursery B, Tuesday. Rehana
At painting time I told Jyoti, "Put on your apron now." She folded her arms and said, "No! I don't want." Then she pushed the apron off the table. I didn't repeat the order. After a minute I held up two aprons and asked, "The blue one with stars, or the yellow one?" Jyoti pointed at the yellow one, pulled it over her head by herself and asked me to tie the back. She painted happily for twenty minutes.
Next: I'll offer two choices at tidy-up time too 🙂

qa.q: What did Jyoti do with the apron when first told to put it on?
qa.a: She pushed the apron off the table.

qa.q: Why do you think Jyoti said no to the apron at first?
qa.a: Being told "now" made it feel like an order, and saying no let her feel in charge of herself.

qa.q: What choice did Rehana make that turned things around?
qa.a: Instead of repeating the order, Rehana offered two aprons, so Jyoti could pick one and put it on happily by herself.

qa.q: How might the other children at the painting table be affected by how Rehana handled it?
qa.a: Painting time stayed calm instead of becoming a struggle, so they could keep painting without waiting or watching a scene.

grounding: A preschooler refuses an apron when ordered but puts one on happily when offered a choice of two.

Morning on the farm outside Wardha. His mother, Urmila, had the lunch tiffin ready for the cotton field. "Darshan, wear your chappals. The stubble will cut your feet." Darshan, five, sat on the doorstep and tucked his feet under him. "No. I'm not wearing."
"Darshan, now."
He shook his head hard.
Urmila put the tiffin down. She fetched his green rubber boots too and set both pairs in front of him. "Chappals or boots? You pick."
Darshan looked at them for a long moment, then jumped into the boots. "I'm wearing BOOTS," he told the hens, and marched off ahead of her.

qa.q: What did Urmila have ready for the cotton field?
qa.a: The lunch tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Darshan tuck his feet under him when told to wear chappals?
qa.a: Being ordered made him want to refuse; hiding his feet was his way of keeping control over what he did.

qa.q: What did Urmila do differently the second time, and why did it work?
qa.a: She set out both chappals and boots and let him pick, so either choice was safe and Darshan felt he was the one deciding.

qa.q: What was it like for Urmila when Darshan refused?
qa.a: She was probably in a hurry with the tiffin ready and worried about the stubble cutting his feet, so the refusal likely tested her patience.

grounding: A five-year-old refuses chappals because he is ordered to, then happily chooses boots when given two safe options.

passage: On a wet morning in Leeds, Nkechi held out the coat. "Bilal, put your coat on. Now, please." Bilal, four, crossed his arms. "No." "It's raining." "NO." He sat down on the doormat. Nkechi took a breath. Then she held up two coats. "Do you want the red coat, or the blue raincoat with the frog?" Bilal looked up. "The frog one," he said, and pushed his arms into the sleeves by himself. "I did it myself!"

qa.q: Which coat did Bilal choose?
qa.a: The blue raincoat with the frog.

qa.q: Why did Bilal say no to putting his coat on?
qa.a: Bilal felt bossed about and stubborn; being told 'now' made him want to show he could decide for himself.

qa.q: What worked for Nkechi, and why?
qa.a: Offering a choice between two coats, both fine, so Bilal felt in charge while still putting a coat on.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt when Bilal sat on the doormat?
qa.a: Nkechi probably felt frustrated and rushed, then chose to take a breath and try another way.

grounding: Shows a preschooler refusing an order, then happily complying when offered a choice between two acceptable coats.

passage: At the playschool, tidy-up time came. "Indu, put the blocks in the box," said Tanuja Miss. Indu, five, turned her back and kept building. "Indu, now." Indu hugged her tower. "It's MY tower." The other children watched. Tanuja Miss knelt beside her. "Should we put away the red blocks first, or the yellow ones?" Indu thought hard. "Yellow," she said, and started dropping them into the box one by one, counting loudly. By the time the red ones went in, she was singing.

qa.q: Which colour blocks did Indu choose to put away first?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: Why did Indu hug her tower when told 'now'?
qa.a: Indu felt pushed and protective; being ordered made her want to hold on and keep control of her own tower.

qa.q: What made tidy-up work in the end?
qa.a: Tanuja Miss knelt down and offered a choice about which colour to put away first, so Indu felt in charge of tidying.

qa.q: How might the other children see Indu's change?
qa.a: They might be surprised to see her go from refusing to singing while tidying.

grounding: Shows a preschooler refusing an instruction, then tidying happily when given a choice between two colours.

passage:
Monday night. "Avni, brush your teeth. Now." Avni, five, ran and hid behind the curtain. Nazia had to carry her to the sink, and both of them ended up cross.
Tuesday night. The same words, the same curtain, tears this time.
Thursday night. Nazia tried something different. She held out two toothbrushes. "Pink one or green one tonight? And do you want to start at the top or the bottom?" Avni came out from behind the curtain. "Green. Bottom!" She brushed by herself, making monster faces in the mirror.

qa.q: Where did Avni hide on Monday night?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: Why did Avni hide when told to brush her teeth 'now'?
qa.a: Avni felt bossed and defiant; the order made her want to show that she could decide.

qa.q: What did Nazia change on Thursday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Nazia offered two choices, which toothbrush and where to start, so Avni felt in control while still brushing.

qa.q: What were Monday and Tuesday like for Nazia?
qa.a: Nazia was probably tired and cross, carrying Avni to the sink and dealing with tears.

grounding: Shows a preschooler resisting an order at bedtime, then brushing happily when given a choice between two options.

Monsoon rain was hammering the roof, and the school van would come in five minutes. Indu, five, stood by the door with one shoe on.

"Put your raincoat on now," said her brother Yash.

"No!" Indu crossed her arms. "I don't want it."

The van honked outside. Yash took a breath. "Okay. Yellow raincoat or the frog one?"

Indu's face changed. "Frog!" She pulled it on herself, zipped it halfway and ran out, splashing in every puddle.

qa.q: Why did Indu cross her arms and say no?
qa.a: Indu felt cross at being told what to do, so refusing felt like keeping her own say.

qa.q: What worked better than ordering Indu, and why?
qa.a: Offering two raincoats let Indu choose, so she felt in charge and happily put one on.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt when the van honked?
qa.a: Yash was probably stressed and hurried, and then relieved when Indu picked the frog raincoat.

grounding: A preschooler refuses an order but complies happily when offered a choice between two acceptable options.

The Diwali lights were already on in the Pune colony when Usha's grandfather Harish came to help her dress for the puja.

"Wear the pink lehenga," he said.

Usha, four, flopped onto the bed. "No. No lehenga."

"Everyone is waiting, Usha."

"I do it myself!" She kicked her feet.

Harish sat down beside her. "Pink lehenga or green frock with the mirrors? You pick."

Usha sat up. "Green!" She wriggled into it by herself, buttons crooked, and marched out to light her diya with a very serious face.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt watching Usha march out in her green frock?

passage:
Kindergarten note, first cold week of December. Written by Mahima, class teacher.
At outdoor time I told Kishore, "Put on your jacket now." He folded his arms. "No! I'm not cold!" His lips were already a little blue.
I said it again, firmly. He sat down on the floor.
Then I held up two things. "Kishore, the green jacket or the brown sweater today? You choose."
He pointed at the green jacket and put it on by himself, zip and all. "I did it myself!"
What I did next: I told his parents about the two choices, and started using them at lunch and tidy-up time too.

qa.q: Which did Kishore choose?
qa.a: Kishore chose the green jacket.

qa.q: Why did Kishore refuse the jacket at first?
qa.a: Kishore felt bossed around and wanted to be in charge, so being ordered made him say no even though he was cold.

qa.q: Why did offering two choices work?
qa.a: It let Kishore feel in charge while both options kept him warm, so he happily put the jacket on himself.

qa.q: How might Kishore's parents use the note?
qa.a: They might feel relieved to learn about the two choices and try them at home for getting dressed.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a preschooler who refuses an order but happily complies when given two acceptable choices.

In the paddy-harvest season, the fields near the village were full of sharp stubble. "Jeevan, wear your slippers," said his big sister Charu.
"No!" Jeevan kicked them away. "I don't want to!"
"Slippers. Now."
He ran off barefoot and stopped at the edge of the field, glaring back.
Charu sighed, then held up two pairs. "Blue slippers, or the old sandals with the frog? You pick."
Jeevan walked back slowly, looked at both and chose the frog sandals. He buckled them himself, tongue sticking out. "I did it!"

qa.q: Which footwear did Jeevan choose?
qa.a: Jeevan chose the old sandals with the frog.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan kick the slippers away?
qa.a: Jeevan felt annoyed at being told what to do and wanted to decide for himself, so the order made him refuse.

qa.q: What did Charu do that worked?
qa.a: Charu offered a choice between two safe options, blue slippers or frog sandals, so Jeevan could choose for himself.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Jeevan buckles the sandals himself?
qa.a: Charu probably feels relieved and amused, glad the choice worked better than giving orders.

grounding: Shows a preschooler who refuses an instruction because it was ordered, then complies happily when given two options.

It was the first hot day of summer on the beach at Cascais. "Rafael, put on your sun hat," said his aunt Beatriz.
Rafael, four, threw the hat in the sand. "No! Me do it!"
"Then do it."
"No hat!"
Beatriz sat down beside him. She held out a yellow hat in one hand and a blue cap in the other. "Yellow hat or blue cap? You choose, and you put it on."
Rafael stared at them, took the blue cap and jammed it on backwards. "Me did it!"
Beatriz turned it the right way round, very gently. He let her.

qa.a: Rafael felt bossed around and wanted to do it himself, so being told made him refuse.

qa.a: Beatriz offered two acceptable choices, the yellow hat or the blue cap, and let Rafael put it on himself.

qa.a: Beatriz is probably amused and relieved, and gently fixes the cap without taking the moment from him.

On the first cold morning of December at Little Steps preschool, Bhupen Sir held out Francis's woolly cap. "Cap on now, Francis. It's chilly outside."
Francis folded his arms. "No! I do it!" He pushed the cap away and stomped to the door without it.
Bhupen Sir paused, then held up two caps. "The red cap or the blue one with the bobble? You choose."
Francis looked at both, grabbed the blue one, tugged it on by himself, crookedly, and marched outside beaming. "I did it!"

qa.q: What two caps did Bhupen Sir offer?
qa.a: The red cap or the blue one with the bobble.

qa.q: Why did Francis push the cap away at first?
qa.a: Being told "Cap on now" made him feel bossed about, and he wanted to be the one in charge, so he felt stubborn about refusing.

qa.q: Which approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering two acceptable caps worked, because Francis still wore a cap but felt he had chosen and done it himself.

qa.q: What would change if Bhupen Sir had kept insisting?
qa.a: Francis would probably have dug in harder, and they might have ended up in a battle at the door instead of a proud march outside.

grounding: Shows a preschooler refusing an instruction and then complying happily when given a choice between two acceptable options.
